subject: Mathematics
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 13 periods = 520 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 8h 40min

tasks_in_class.description: Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers (multiplicands and multipliers) to get given products; fill remaining white boxes with appropriate products. Second puzzle: identify numbers using row and column products in orange and blue boxes.

time_bands.activity: Pose the question: if you know the answer to a multiplication, can you find what was multiplied? Let pairs share one example each from their mental tables — this readies the backward-reasoning stance the grid will demand.

Students work on Mystery Matrix, p.184 ("Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers … get given products…."). Each pair fills in missing multiplicands, then completes the white product boxes. For the second puzzle, pairs use the orange and blue row/column products as constraints to identify the hidden numbers.
Pairs share one cell they found hardest to fill and explain the reasoning they used. Class discusses whether there could be more than one valid answer for any yellow box.

periods.teacher_notes: The grid structure forces backward reasoning — students must think 'which two 1-digit numbers give this product?' rather than forward computation. A common error is to fill yellow boxes with any pair that produces the right cell product while ignoring the row or column constraint; prompt students to check every row and column product before settling on an answer.

periods.activity_title: Groups of Ten: Arrays, Tens Language, and the Hundred

tasks_in_class.description: Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation and write the answer: 2×10=2 Tens=__, 5×10=__Tens=__, 8×10=__Tens=__.
What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __? (extending the ×10 pattern to 10 groups of 10 = 100)

time_bands.activity: Students draw dots arranged in rows of 10 on squared paper — 2 rows, then 5 rows, then 8 rows. They count the total and write the matching statement: '2 rows of 10 = 2 Tens = 20'.

Open Times-10, p.184 ("Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation…."). Students match each dot-array picture to the multiplication statement and fill in the Tens language and numeral.
Move to Times-10, p.185 ("What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __?...."). Students draw 10 rows of 10, count the dots, complete the statement, and discuss with a partner why 10 Tens makes a Hundred.

periods.teacher_notes: The language '2 Tens = 20' is doing important place-value work — it links the multiplication act to the positional name. A common error is writing '2×10 = 20 Tens' (attaching the Tens label to the product numeral instead of the count of groups); model the phrasing 'two groups of ten = 2 Tens = 20' deliberately.

periods.activity_title: Splitting 15 into 10 and 5: Building the Times-15 Table

tasks_in_class.description: Count pebbles in a 5×15 arrangement; complete: 5×15 = 5×10 and 5×5 = __ + __ = __.
Construct a times-15 table (1×15 through 10×15) using the 10×15 pebble arrangement, splitting columns into 10 and 5.
What patterns do you see in the times-15 table?

homework.description: Compare the times-15 table with the times-5 table. What similarities and differences do you notice? Complete the difference column (15−5=10, 30−10=20, ...).

time_bands.activity: Students use pebbles or counters to form a 5×15 arrangement on their desks. They separate the 15 columns into a group of 10 and a group of 5, count each part, and complete Constructing Tables, p.185 ("Count pebbles in a 5×15 arrangement….") writing the split-addition sentence.

Using the same splitting idea, students build each row of the times-15 table from 1×15 through 10×15 per Constructing Tables, p.186 ("Construct a times-15 table … splitting columns into 10 and 5."). Each entry is written as (N×10) + (N×5) = answer.

Constructing Tables Q1, p.186 ("What patterns do you see in the times-15 table?"). Students share observations — products end in 0 or 5, increase by 15 each time — and the class lists two clear pattern statements.

periods.teacher_notes: The split into 10 and 5 is a concrete instance of the distributive property; name it in plain words ('we break 15 into a ten-part and a five-part') without using the algebraic term. A common error is adding the two partial products incorrectly; encourage students to verify by counting all pebbles before recording.

periods.activity_title: Comparing Tables 11–20 and Discovering Cross-Table Patterns

tasks_in_class.description: Construct other times-tables for numbers from 11 to 20, as done for 15.
Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12, and so on. Share your observations.

time_bands.activity: Small groups each pick a different table (11 through 20) and construct it using the split-into-10-and-unit strategy, per Constructing Tables Q3, p.186 ("Construct other times-tables for numbers from 11 to 20…."). Each group writes out all ten entries and posts their table for the class to see.

Whole class compares: Constructing Tables Q4, p.186 ("Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12…."). Students examine pairs of tables (e.g. times-2 next to times-12) and articulate what every times-12 entry has in common with the corresponding times-2 entry, recording at least two observations.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked through the times-15 table construction (splitting into tens and units) have the strategy they need to tackle any table from 11 to 20. The cross-table comparison is the conceptual payoff: guide students to see that times-12 = times-2 + times-10, not merely that the numbers are 'bigger by 10'. A common error is stating the difference as 'ten more' without specifying per row.
materials: Large paper or chart strips for group tables

section_titles: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
periods.activity_title: Doubling Half: the Splitting Strategy for Even Multipliers

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187
tasks_in_class.description: 6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why? (explain the splitting-and-doubling reasoning from the wheel arrangement)

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188
tasks_in_class.description: Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling? Try! What other times-tables can be constructed by splitting into equal groups and doubling? Give examples.

time_bands.activity: Students look at the wheel diagram in the textbook and work in pairs to explain why 6×14 equals double of 6×7, using Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187 ("6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why?...."). Pairs write the explanation in their own words before sharing with the class.

Students attempt Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188 ("Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling?…."). They build the table entry by entry using the doubling route, then list at least three other even-multiplier tables for which the same trick works, giving a specific example for each.

periods.teacher_notes: The splitting-and-doubling strategy works for any even multiplier; the key insight is that half of 14 is 7, so the known times-7 table is reusable. A common error is trying to apply the same strategy to odd multipliers like 13 or 15 — ask students to check whether the multiplier halves to a whole number before deciding to use this route.

periods.activity_title: Tens Language for 2-Digit Numbers: Multiplying by 10 and by 20

tasks_in_class.description: 10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__. Discuss in grade what happens when we take several groups of 10.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Multiples of 10, p.188 ("Find the answers: a) 15×10=__Tens=__…."), writing each product in Tens language first, then as a numeral. They use the flat-and-rod imagery from the textbook to visualise each group.
Class discussion using Multiples of 10, p.188 ("10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__…."). Students articulate what taking several groups of 10 does to the count of Tens.
Students work independently on Now think and answer, p.189 ("Answer: a) 21×10, b) 42×10, c) 65×10…."), writing their working in Tens language before stating the answer. A few share their approach.

periods.teacher_notes: The Tens-language step ('14 Tens = 140') is the bridge between the multiplication act and place-value understanding; insist students write it before the numeral. A common error is writing 14×10 = 1410 (concatenating digits rather than shifting); having students count Tens aloud corrects this.

periods.activity_title: Multiplying by Multiples of 10: From 20 to 80

time_bands.activity: Review the three child voices from the textbook's 12×20 page. Students explain in their own words which of the three strategies they find most natural, writing one sentence justifying their choice.

Students work through Solve the following problems, p.190 ("24×40=__, 13×30=__, 50×60=__, 43×60=__, 70×80=__…."), showing step-by-step working for each using their chosen strategy. Pairs compare methods for 43×60 and discuss which is more efficient.

periods.teacher_notes: Students should recognise that multiplying by 40 is the same as multiplying by 4 and then by 10 (or by 4 Tens). A common error is multiplying the non-zero digits correctly but writing one zero instead of two in the final product (e.g. 24×40 = 960 written as 96); prompt students to check by estimating ('24 is close to 25, and 25×40=1000, so 960 is reasonable').

section_titles: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
periods.activity_title: Area Model and Grouping Table: 2-Digit Multiplication and Division

tasks_in_class.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
tasks_in_class.description: Find 15×14 using the area-model grid (toy train: 15 coaches × 14 seats). How many children can be seated?

tasks_in_class.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
tasks_in_class.description: Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table. How many coaches for 324 children? Identify the remainder.

homework.description: Solve: a) 25×34, b) 16×43, c) 68×12, d) 39×13, e) 125÷15, f) 94÷11, g) 440÷22, h) 508÷18. Also identify remainder (if any) in division problems.

time_bands.activity: Students draw the area-model grid for 15×14 on squared paper, labelling the four sub-rectangles (10×10, 10×4, 5×10, 5×4), and complete A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191 ("Find 15×14 using the area-model grid…."). They add the four partial products to answer how many children can be seated.

Students set up the repeated-subtraction table for 324÷14 per A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191 ("Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table…."), subtracting multiples of 14 systematically until the remainder is less than 14. They name the quotient and the remainder.

periods.teacher_notes: The area model makes each partial product visible as a rectangular region; students sometimes add only two of the four sub-rectangles. Remind them to label all four cells before adding. For division, the term 'remainder' is introduced here — stress that the remainder must be smaller than the divisor, a check students can self-apply.

section_titles: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
periods.activity_title: Hundreds Language: Multiplying by 100 and Bridging to Thousands

tasks_in_class.description: 10×100=10 Hundreds=1000. What happens when we put 10 Hundreds together? Complete: 12×100=__, 15×100=__, 27×100=__, 70×100=__.
We Know: 80×100=8000. Find: 80×50=__, 40×50=__. (Use relationship between ×100 and ×50)

time_bands.activity: Using Dienes flats (or sketches of them), students count groups of 100 and complete Multiples of 100, p.192 ("Complete: 3×100=__Hundreds=__…."), writing each product in Hundreds language before recording the numeral.
Students complete Multiples of 100, p.192 ("10×100=10 Hundreds=1000….") and discuss what bridging 10 Hundreds means: a thousand. They extend to 12×100, 15×100, and beyond.
Now answer (We Know/Find), p.193 ("We Know: 80×100=8000. Find: 80×50=__, 40×50=__…."). Students use the halving relationship between ×100 and ×50 to derive the answers and share their reasoning.

periods.teacher_notes: The Hundreds-language step mirrors the Tens-language work earlier in the chapter; use that parallel explicitly to build confidence. A common error is writing 12×100 = 1200 correctly but then writing 12×200 = 1200 (not doubling); T-24 in the unit that follows addresses this directly, so it need not be fully resolved here.

section_titles: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
periods.activity_title: Three Ways to See 11×200: Patterns Across Multiples of 100

tasks_in_class.description: 11×200 shown three ways. Share what you notice. Then: 11×100=__, 11×200=__, 22×100=__, 22×200=__. What do you notice about any number times-100s?

time_bands.activity: Students study the three representations of 11×200 in Answer the following questions, p.194 ("11×200 shown three ways. Share what you notice…."), then complete the four related products and write one sentence describing what they observe about multiplying any number by a multiple of 100.

Students work through Set A/B/C, p.195 ("Find answers in Set A … use relationships to find Set B … answer Set C…."). They compute Set A independently, use those results to fill Set B without fresh computation, and then tackle Set C by selecting the appropriate relationship.

periods.teacher_notes: The three-strategy presentation of 11×200 models mathematical flexibility; prompt students to say in words what each strategy does before they evaluate which is easiest. For Set B, students should not recompute from scratch — if they are doing so, ask them to look at how Set B entries relate to Set A entries they have already found.

periods.activity_title: Rice Sacks and Snake-Boat Races: Dividing by 10 and 100

tasks_in_class.description: Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks, b) 600 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks. If sack weighs 100 kg, 600÷100=__. Write: 60÷10=__, 600÷10=__, 600÷100=__.
1. Manku sees 870 bananas; each bunch has 10. How many bunches? 2. Rukhma Bi distributes ₹1000 equally among 10 grandchildren. How much each? Write the division statement.

time_bands.activity: Students work through the rice-sack story in Dividing by 10 and 100, p.197 ("Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks…."), acting out the packing by grouping counters into tens. They write all three division statements.
Students complete the pattern grid in Find the answers, p.198 ("40÷10=__, 400÷10=__, 400÷100=__….") and share their observations about how the number of zeros in the divisor changes the answer.
Think and answer, p.198 ("Manku sees 870 bananas … Rukhma Bi distributes ₹1000…."). Students write a division statement for each story and solve using the place-value pattern they just identified.

periods.teacher_notes: Division by 10 reverses the multiplication-by-10 act: one Tens group collapses to its unit count. Students sometimes treat ÷10 as ÷2 (halving); the pattern grid makes the relationship explicit. Encourage students to write the full division statement (dividend ÷ divisor = quotient) for word problems to build the habit of identifying all three components.

periods.activity_title: Large-Number Operations: Consolidating Multiplication and Division

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit the area-model grid and repeated-subtraction table strategies (introduced with the toy-train and coach stories). Students describe in one sentence each how they would set up a 3-digit by 2-digit multiplication and a 3-digit by 2-digit division.

Students work through Let Us Solve, p.197 ("a) 237×28, b) 140×16, c) 389×57, d) 807÷24, e) 692÷33, f) 996÷45…."), showing full working and identifying the remainder for each division problem. Pairs check each other's answers.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit is primarily consolidation of the area-model and repeated-subtraction methods on larger numbers. A common error in 3-digit multiplication is misaligning partial products; encourage students to use squared paper and write each partial product in its own row before adding. For division, a remainder larger than the divisor is a reliable self-check signal.

section_titles: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
periods.activity_title: Transport Stories, Coin Puzzles, and a Multiplication Pattern

tasks_in_class.description: Punjab Mail: a) 3 coaches carried 96 passengers — how many per coach? b) Train now has 24 coaches, each carrying 72 passengers — how many can travel?
Chilika lake trip (8 people): bus ticket ₹60 each, boat ride ₹1200 for all. How much per person? (multi-step)

Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes, Munna ₹50 notes, Balu ₹20 notes, Chinnu ₹5 coins, Sansu ₹2 coins. a) How many notes/coins each needs; b) who gets no change; c) how long to count Chinnu's coins?

Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154, 13×13=169, 11×12=132. In each case, spot a pattern in the two numbers and their product (coloured digits). For what other multiplication problems does this pattern hold? Find 5 such examples.

homework.description: Find multiplication and division sentences in the number grid. Shade them. How many can you find? (3 given: 250×4=1000, 50×20=1000, 525÷5=105; find more)

time_bands.activity: Students solve the two Punjab Mail problems in Let Us Solve Q1, p.198 ("a) 3 coaches carried 96 passengers….") and the Chilika lake multi-step problem in Let Us Solve Q4, p.199 ("bus ticket ₹60 each, boat ride ₹1200 for all…."), writing the full operation for each step.

Students tackle Chinnu's Coins Q1, p.201 ("Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes…."), computing how many notes or coins each character needs, identifying who pays exactly, and estimating counting time for Chinnu's coins.

Students study the four given products in Chinnu's Coins Q2, p.201 ("Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154…."), describe the digit pattern they see, and find at least two further examples that fit the same pattern before the unit closes.

periods.teacher_notes: The Chilika lake problem requires two operations — multiplying individual tickets then adding the shared boat cost — so students should plan the steps before computing. For the coin puzzle, ₹750 is not divisible by 2, so Sansu cannot pay exactly; pushing students to check divisibility before computing is the embedded mathematical habit. The closing pattern question is open-ended — two examples in class is a realistic target; the full five are a satisfying stretch.

items.prompt: A multiplication grid has two rows and two columns. The product of the first row is 12, and the product of the second row is 18. The product of the first column is 6, and the product of the second column is 36. Each cell holds a 1-digit number. Fill in all four cells of the grid.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: First row: 2 and 6; Second row: 3 and 6. (First column product: 2×3=6 ✓; Second column product: 6×6=36 ✓; Row 1 product: 2×6=12 ✓; Row 2 product: 3×6=18 ✓.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use row and column products as constraints: find which 1-digit pairs multiply to each product and check both the row and column conditions together.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student list all pairs of 1-digit numbers that give each row product, then check which pair also satisfies the column; stretch: ask whether there is any other solution.

exercise.description: Fill yellow boxes with 1-digit numbers (multiplicands and multipliers) to get given products; fill remaining white boxes with appropriate products. Second puzzle: identify numbers using row and column products in orange and blue boxes.

items.prompt: A student arranges dots in 6 equal rows. Each row has 10 dots. Which statement correctly describes the total?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the number of rows to get the number of Tens groups, then write the numeral as that many tens.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student is writing the group size (10) as the number of Tens instead of counting the number of groups (6).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is adding 6 and 10 instead of multiplying, arriving at 16.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is attaching the Tens label to the final product numeral (60) rather than to the count of groups.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically count the rows of dots and write '__ rows = __ Tens'; stretch: ask them to draw the array for 9×10 and write the matching statement.

exercise.description: Match each problem with the appropriate pictorial representation and write the answer: 2×10=2 Tens=__, 5×10=__Tens=__, 8×10=__Tens=__.

items.prompt: Use the splitting method to find 4 × 15. Write your working as: 4 × 15 = 4 × 10 + 4 × 5 = ___ + ___ = ___.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 15 into 10 and 5, multiply each part separately, then add the two partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student arrange counters in a 4×15 grid and separate the last 5 columns from the first 10 before counting each part; stretch: use the same method to find 7×15.

exercise.description: Construct a times-15 table (1×15 through 10×15) using the 10×15 pebble arrangement, splitting columns into 10 and 5.

items.section_title: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
items.prompt: Priya wants to find 5 × 14 using the splitting-and-doubling method. She splits 14 into two equal groups. Which working is correct?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split the even multiplier (14) into two equal halves (7 each), compute one group, then double the result.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student doubled the full product instead of halving the multiplier first — they have applied the doubling step before the halving step.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student halved 14 to get 7 but then added 5 (the other factor) instead of multiplying and doubling.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student incorrectly split both factors rather than only the multiplier, using 7×7 as the base computation.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student first find 5×7 with counters, then combine two identical groups; stretch: use the same strategy to find 8×14.

exercise.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.188
exercise.description: Can we construct the times-14 table by splitting and doubling? Try! What other times-tables can be constructed by splitting into equal groups and doubling? Give examples.

items.prompt: A student says: 'Ten groups of 10 make 100, so 10 Tens = 1 Hundred.' Is this correct? Explain why using the words Tens and Hundreds.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes, it is correct. 10 × 10 = 10 Tens = 100, and 100 is the same as 1 Hundred. So 10 Tens and 1 Hundred name the same amount.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count 10 groups of 10 dots to reach 100, then rename 10 Tens as 1 Hundred using place-value language.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw 10 rows of 10 dots and count; stretch: ask what 20 Tens would be called.

exercise.description: What is 10×10 = __ Tens = __? (extending the ×10 pattern to 10 groups of 10 = 100)

items.prompt: Look at the two facts: 3 × 15 = 45 and 3 × 5 = 15. How much more is 3 × 15 than 3 × 5? Will the same difference hold for 7 × 15 and 7 × 5? Explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 × 15 is 30 more than 3 × 5, because 15 − 5 = 10, so 3 groups of that difference = 3 × 10 = 30. For 7 × 15 and 7 × 5 the difference is 7 × 10 = 70. The difference is always (the multiplier) × 10.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: The difference between any times-15 entry and the corresponding times-5 entry equals the row number multiplied by 10, since 15 − 5 = 10.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write 3×15 and 3×5 side by side and subtract; stretch: ask for the difference between 9×15 and 9×5 without computing each product.

exercise.description: What patterns do you see in the times-15 table?

items.prompt: The times-2 table gives: 1×2=2, 2×2=4, 3×2=6 … The times-12 table gives: 1×12=12, 2×12=24, 3×12=36 … How does each times-12 entry relate to the matching times-2 entry?

options.label: A
options.text: Each times-12 entry is 10 times the matching times-2 entry.

options.label: B
options.text: Each times-12 entry equals the matching times-2 entry plus 10 times that row number.

options.label: C
options.text: Each times-12 entry equals the matching times-2 entry multiplied by 6.

options.label: D
options.text: Each times-12 entry equals the matching times-2 entry plus 10.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each times-12 entry equals the matching times-2 entry plus 10 times that row number. For example, 3×12 = 3×2 + 3×10 = 6 + 30 = 36.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: 12 = 2 + 10, so N×12 = N×2 + N×10; the extra amount grows with each row.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is confusing the relationship between times-1 and times-10 tables with the times-2 and times-12 relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student sees 12 as 2×6 and incorrectly concludes the times-12 entry is 6 times the times-2 entry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student notices that 12−2=10 and adds a fixed 10 to every entry, ignoring that the extra amount scales with the row number.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: write 1×12 and 1×2 side by side and subtract; repeat for rows 2 and 3 to see the pattern grow; stretch: predict the difference for row 8 without computing 8×12.

exercise.description: Compare times-1 with times-11, times-2 with times-12, and so on. Share your observations.

items.section_title: Making tables by splitting into equal groups
items.prompt: Rajan says he can use splitting and doubling to find 9 × 16 but not 9 × 15. Is he right? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Rajan is right. 16 is even, so it can be split into two equal groups of 8: 9×16 = double of 9×8 = 2×72 = 144. 15 is odd and cannot be split into two equal whole-number groups, so the splitting-and-doubling strategy does not apply directly.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Splitting and doubling works only when the multiplier is even, so it halves to a whole number.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to try splitting 15 counters into two equal groups and see what happens; stretch: ask how they would handle 9×15 if not by doubling.

exercise.book_ref: Making tables by splitting into equal groups, p.187
exercise.description: 6×14 = Double of 6×7. Why? (explain the splitting-and-doubling reasoning from the wheel arrangement)

items.prompt: A student notices that 10 × 10 = 100. She then claims that 20 × 10 = 200 because '20 is double 10, so the answer is double 100'. Which statement best explains why she is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: Because adding a zero to 20 gives 200.

options.label: C
options.text: Because 20 is 10 more than 10, so the answer is 10 more than 100.

options.label: D
options.text: Because any number multiplied by 10 always ends in two zeros.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 20 × 10 = 2 Tens × 10 = 2 × 100 = 200, so doubling 10 doubles the product.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Express 20 as 2 Tens; then 2 Tens × 10 = 2 × (10 × 10) = 2 × 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is using a digit-manipulation rule ('append a zero') without understanding the place-value reason.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is treating the multiplier as an addend, adding 10 to the product instead of doubling it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is overgeneralising — single-digit numbers times 10 end in one zero, not two; the claim is false as a general rule.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to draw 20 rows of 10 dots and group them into pairs of 10 rows; stretch: use the same reasoning to explain why 30×10 = 300.

exercise.description: 10×10=__; 2 times (double of) 10×10=__. Discuss in grade what happens when we take several groups of 10.

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: A student writes: 11 × 100 = 1100 and 11 × 200 = 2200. She says: 'When I doubled the hundreds, the answer doubled.' Does the same pattern hold for 11 × 300? Show your working and explain.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. 11 × 300 = 11 × 3 × 100 = 33 × 100 = 3300. Since 300 is three times 100, the answer is three times 1100. The pattern is: multiplying by N hundreds gives N times the answer for multiplying by one hundred.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write the hundreds multiplier as N × 100, compute N × the base product, because multiplication is associative.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first find 11×100, then count how many hundreds are in 300, and multiply; stretch: ask them to predict 11×500 without computing step by step.

exercise.description: 11×200 shown three ways. Share what you notice. Then: 11×100=__, 11×200=__, 22×100=__, 22×200=__. What do you notice about any number times-100s?

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: A student knows that 14 × 100 = 1400. She uses this to find 14 × 500. Which working is correct?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Write 500 as 100 × 5, use the known result 14×100=1400, then multiply by 5.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added the multiplier (500) to the known product instead of using the multiplicative relationship.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student dropped the hundreds entirely and only multiplied 14 by the leading digit 5.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student treated 500 as 100 × 10 instead of 100 × 5, over-multiplying by a factor of 2.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first write 500 = 5 × 100 and then substitute the known value of 14×100; stretch: use the same approach to find 14×250.

items.prompt: A student finds: 40 ÷ 10 = 4, 400 ÷ 10 = 40, 400 ÷ 100 = 4. She says: 'Dividing by 10 removes one zero from the number, and dividing by 100 removes two zeros.' Is she right? Give one example that supports her claim and one that tests its limits.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She is right for multiples of 10 and 100. Supporting example: 600 ÷ 10 = 60 (one zero removed), 600 ÷ 100 = 6 (two zeros removed). Testing the limits: 870 ÷ 10 = 87 — here we cannot simply 'remove' a zero because 870 ends in one zero; we must think in Tens (87 Tens) instead. The zero-removal shortcut is reliable only when the number ends in at least as many zeros as the divisor.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Dividing by 10 reduces the number of Tens by a factor of 10; dividing by 100 reduces the number of Hundreds — this is the place-value reason the shortcut works.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: have the student use counters grouped in tens and physically remove one grouping level; stretch: ask what happens with 850 ÷ 10 and whether removing a zero gives the right answer.

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: A student notices: 12 × 13 = 156 and 11 × 14 = 154. She says the second product is 2 less. She then tries 10 × 15 = 150 and finds it is 4 less than 12 × 13. Does the product keep decreasing by 2 each time one factor goes down by 1 and the other goes up by 1 (starting from 12 × 13)? Check one more step and describe what you notice.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Yes. Starting from 12×13=156: 11×14=154 (−2), 10×15=150 (−4), 9×16=144 (−6). The product decreases by 2 more each time — the decreases are 2, 4, 6 … (not a constant drop but an increasing drop). The pattern shows the product falls, and by more each step.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute each product and subtract consecutive results to see the pattern of differences.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to compute 9×16 and compare it to 10×15; stretch: ask whether the product will ever reach zero and how many steps that might take.

exercise.description: Observe: 12×13=156, 11×14=154, 13×13=169, 11×12=132. In each case, spot a pattern in the two numbers and their product (coloured digits). For what other multiplication problems does this pattern hold? Find 5 such examples.

items.prompt: Find the value of 17 × 10. Write your answer in Tens language first, then as a numeral.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the groups (17) to name the Tens, then write the numeral by placing those Tens in the hundreds and tens columns.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has used the group size (10) as the Tens count instead of the number of groups (17).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has written the digits 1, 0, 7 by concatenating 10 and 7 rather than multiplying.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has concatenated 17 and 10 to form 1710 rather than recognising 17 Tens = 170.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 17 rows of 10 dots and count; stretch: find 17×20 using the same Tens-language step.

items.section_title: Multiples of 100: multiplying by 100 and multiples of 100
items.prompt: Complete the statement: 18 × 100 = ___ Hundreds = ___.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count the groups (18) to name the Hundreds, then write the numeral by placing 18 in the thousands and hundreds columns.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has written the group size (100) as the Hundreds count instead of the number of groups (18).
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has concatenated 18 and 100 by writing only the first non-zero digits, arriving at 118.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has concatenated 18 and 100 directly to form 18100.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 18 Dienes flat blocks and count aloud '1 Hundred, 2 Hundreds … 18 Hundreds'; stretch: complete 18×200 using the same approach.

exercise.description: 10×100=10 Hundreds=1000. What happens when we put 10 Hundreds together? Complete: 12×100=__, 15×100=__, 27×100=__, 70×100=__.

items.prompt: A school orders 36 pencil boxes. Each box holds 10 pencils. How many pencils does the school have in all?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 360 pencils.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw 36 rows of 10 dots or use Dienes rods; stretch: change the order to 36 boxes of 20 pencils and find the new total.

items.prompt: A factory packs candles in boxes of 30. If there are 24 boxes, how many candles are there in all?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply 24 by 3 first to get 72, then multiply by 10 to get 720.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first find 24×3 and then attach a zero; stretch: find 24×60 using the same steps.

items.section_title: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
items.prompt: A toy-train display has 12 coaches. Each coach has 13 seats. Use the area-model method to find the total number of seats.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split one factor into tens and units, compute two partial products using the area model, then add them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw the area-model grid with cells labelled 10×10, 10×3, 2×10, 2×3 and fill each; stretch: find 23×13 using the same grid.

exercise.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
exercise.description: Find 15×14 using the area-model grid (toy train: 15 coaches × 14 seats). How many children can be seated?

items.section_title: A Day at the Transport Museum: 2-digit multiplication and division
items.prompt: A museum has 195 visitors. They are seated in groups of 13 for a show. How many full groups can be formed, and how many visitors are left over?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15 full groups, 0 visitors left over. 195 ÷ 13 = 15 remainder 0. Verification: 15 × 13 = 195.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the repeated-subtraction table: subtract multiples of 13 from 195 until the remainder is less than 13.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: start the table at 5×13=65 and keep subtracting; stretch: change the total to 200 and find the new quotient and remainder.

exercise.book_ref: A Day at the Transport Museum, p.191
exercise.description: Find 324÷14 using the repeated-subtraction table. How many coaches for 324 children? Identify the remainder.

items.prompt: A store has 540 oranges. The oranges are packed into bags of 10. How many bags are filled?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: 540 = 54 Tens; dividing by 10 gives 54.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: group 540 counters into tens and count the groups; stretch: if the bags held 100 oranges each, how many bags would be needed?

exercise.description: Rice sack problems: a) 60 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks, b) 600 kg ÷ 10 kg sacks = __ sacks. If sack weighs 100 kg, 600÷100=__. Write: 60÷10=__, 600÷10=__, 600÷100=__.

items.prompt: Rani has 480 beads. She shares them equally among 10 friends. How many beads does each friend receive? Write the division statement.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 48 beads each. Division statement: 480 ÷ 10 = 48.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: 480 = 48 Tens; dividing by 10 gives 48.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write 480 as __ Tens and then say how many Tens each friend gets; stretch: if she shared the same 480 beads among 20 friends, how many each?

exercise.description: 1. Manku sees 870 bananas; each bunch has 10. How many bunches? 2. Rukhma Bi distributes ₹1000 equally among 10 grandchildren. How much each? Write the division statement.

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: A train has 4 coaches. Each coach carries 96 passengers. How many passengers can the train carry in all?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Split 96 into 90 and 6, multiply each part by 4, then add the partial products.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: draw an area model splitting 96 into 90 and 6; stretch: find how many passengers if the train had 6 such coaches.

exercise.description: Punjab Mail: a) 3 coaches carried 96 passengers — how many per coach? b) Train now has 24 coaches, each carrying 72 passengers — how many can travel?

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: Six friends go on a lake trip. Each bus ticket costs ₹50. The boat ride costs ₹600 for the whole group. What is the total amount each person pays for both the bus and the boat?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each person pays ₹150. Bus: ₹50 per person. Boat: ₹600 ÷ 6 = ₹100 per person. Total: ₹50 + ₹100 = ₹150.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the per-person boat cost by dividing the total boat cost by the number of people, then add the individual bus cost.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to solve the bus cost and boat cost as two separate steps before adding; stretch: find the total the whole group spends.

exercise.description: Chilika lake trip (8 people): bus ticket ₹60 each, boat ride ₹1200 for all. How much per person? (multi-step)

items.section_title: Chinnu's Coins: money problems and pattern exploration
items.prompt: A museum entry ticket costs ₹500. Kavya pays using ₹50 notes only. How many ₹50 notes does she need? Will she get any change?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: She needs 10 notes of ₹50 (because 10 × ₹50 = ₹500). She gets no change.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the ticket price by the note value: 500 ÷ 50 = 10.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to skip-count by 50 until reaching 500 and count the steps; stretch: ask how many ₹20 notes would be needed for the same ticket and whether ₹20 divides 500 exactly.

exercise.description: Ticket costs ₹750. Bujji uses ₹200 notes, Munna ₹50 notes, Balu ₹20 notes, Chinnu ₹5 coins, Sansu ₹2 coins. a) How many notes/coins each needs; b) who gets no change; c) how long to count Chinnu's coins?
